label: input token h during the copy phase
explanation: Fires whenever the fed-back input token is h during the copy phase (t > L). It fires on every such step (precision 1.0) with typical activation around 0.7-0.8 of max. The strongest activations come on repeated h, e.g. an h right after another h or a second h in the sequence (top examples hh in the copy, ~0.85-1.0). It also fires weakly (~0.12-0.15) on h in the original phase at early positions (t=1-3). Those h steps make up most of the misses, along with tiny activations on the first copied token at some steps, and together they hold about 1% of activation mass. It does not fire at the delimiter or on other tokens; magnitude is roughly flat across L and recall position.

issues: The core claim holds on the test split. (phase==2)&(in_tok==h) has precision 1.0 (0 false positives on test), F1 0.963 and mass recall 0.986. Firing on any non-h copy-phase token has precision 0.0015, so it is not a real pattern.

The explanation gets the makeup of the misses backwards. Original-phase h accounts for only 2.99% of active steps (recall 0.030, mass 0.6%). Weak firing on non-h copy-phase tokens is larger, at 4.08% of active steps (~4000 test steps, mass 0.7%). So the misses are not 'mostly' original-phase h, and 'a few tiny activations' undersells the other group.

Most of those non-h copy misses come at recall_idx==1, the first copy step (recall 0.028), with activation around 0.10-0.13. Some come one step before an h is fed in. Neither group is predictable: precision is 0.006 for the first-step group and 0.018 for the 'next input is h' group, and adding rel_tok(1)==h drops F1 to 0.71. So they are low-magnitude noise rather than a class the predicate should cover.
'Fires weakly on h in the original phase at early positions' overstates it. h at t<=3 is active only 4.2% of the time (precision 0.042). These are rare, sporadic activations, not reliable firing.

The repeated-hh claim is only weakly supported. hh in the copy phase has mass recall 0.0285 against recall 0.0258, so its mean activation is about 10% above the h-in-copy average. That fits 'slightly stronger' but is not strong evidence for 0.85-1.0.
